prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 6 of part 2 (classification) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: credit card fraud data from OpenML (id 1597, about 285,000 transactions, features `V1` to `V28` are anonymized principal components plus `Amount`). The notebook keeps the 492 frauds and samples legitimate transactions for 10,000 rows, about 5 percent fraud. `StratifiedShuffleSplit` draws 10 independent splits with 1,500 training rows (about 74 frauds) and 500 test rows (about 25 frauds); a note explains why stratification can understate the variability on new data. A skore `ComparisonReport` of two `CrossValidationReport`s compares `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` and TabICL (`TabAPIClassifier`, `n_estimators=1`), both with default hyperparameters. In the browser, `fetch_openml` needs the `pyodide_http.patch_urllib()` setup cell.

Results of the reference run: at the default threshold of 0.5, both models catch about 21 of the 25 frauds of a test set and block fewer than one legitimate payment; precision and recall differences are within the spread. ROC curves hug the top left corner and look flattering on imbalanced data; PR curves are more demanding, with precision near 1 up to a recall of about 0.8 for both. These curves only depend on the order of the scores. A note warns that production fraud is about 30 times rarer, so the PR curve and the probabilities would change. Gradient boosting's test log loss is almost twice TabICL's, while the Brier score barely separates them since it caps the cost of a confident mistake. A reliability diagram with log scales and quantile bins (100 transactions each) shows gradient boosting predicting a few in a million for low-risk bins whose observed fraud rate is 1 or 2 percent, about three orders of magnitude off, while TabICL sits much closer to the diagonal, though still above it.

Decision rule from the costs: accepting a legitimate payment earns 2 percent of its amount, accepting a fraud loses its amount plus 20 euros, blocking a legitimate payment costs 10 euros, blocking a fraud costs nothing. A payment of amount `a` should be blocked when its probability exceeds `(10 + 0.02 a) / (30 + 1.02 a)`, between 2 and 33 percent. The rule needs no data but reads probabilities as true risks, so it needs calibration. It earns about 150 euros more per test set than the default threshold for TabICL (mostly from one test set), about 50 more for gradient boosting, which puts few payments in the 2 to 50 percent range.

Why TabICL is better calibrated: gradient boosting minimizes the log loss on its 1,500 training rows, where its trees isolate the 74 frauds and push probabilities toward 0 or 1 (training log loss near zero against about 0.07 on test), so it overfits. Its 5 worst test rows include on average 2.6 frauds scored below 0.1 percent, against 0.2 for TabICL. TabICL's log loss was minimized during pretraining on rows held out of the context, as for the prediction intervals of the pinball loss notebook. Calibration is not guaranteed and follows the context's fraud rate. Gradient boosting can be scored on held-out rows through early stopping, a random search on the log loss or `CalibratedClassifierCV`, all taking rows from the same few frauds.

Place in the course: after TabICL_decision_boundary; the next notebook, TabICL_business_metric, tunes thresholds with a business metric; questions about threshold tuning get a short answer and a pointer there. Related scikit-learn course material: classification metrics, stratification and baselines (Evaluating Model Performance), gradient boosting (Ensemble Models).
